arXiv:2611.21118v1 [math.AG] 16 Nov 2026

Intersection theory and Chern classes on normal varieties II

Adrian Langer
November 16, 2026
Abstract

We prove a uniform bound linear in the rank for the local correction terms in the Riemann–Roch formula for reflexive sheaves on normal surfaces over algebraically closed fields of arbitrary characteristic. We also establish the usual tensor and symmetric-power formulas for second Chern characters and prove Wahl’s asymptotic Riemann–Roch conjecture and its higher-rank generalization. These results yield second Chern classes of reflexive sheaves on arbitrary normal projective varieties, compatible with pullback by finite surjective morphisms. We characterize their discriminants as infima of normalized discriminants of compatible vector bundles on smooth alterations. As applications we prove Bogomolov’s inequality, effective restriction and boundedness theorems on normal projective varieties, a Miyaoka-type inequality, and a Segre-class criterion for bigness of reflexive sheaves on normal surfaces.

Introduction

In [Wah93] Wahl introduced relative Chern classes of rank 22 vector bundles on resolutions of complex surface singularities. In [Lan00] and [Lan25] we extended these classes to arbitrary rank and characteristic, and used them to construct Chern classes of reflexive sheaves on normal surfaces over an algebraically closed field. The most important feature of these classes is that they behave like orbifold Chern classes and they are useful in asymptotic Riemann–Roch computations. For a normal proper surface XX and a reflexive coherent 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of rank rr, these classes satisfy also the Riemann–Roch formula

χ⁡(X,ℰ)=12​c1​(ℰ).(c1​(ℰ)−KX)−∫Xc2​(ℰ)+r​χ​(X,𝒪X)+∑x∈SingXa⁡(x,ℰ),\chi(X,{\mathcal{E}})=\frac{1}{2}c_{1}({\mathcal{E}}).(c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})-K_{X})-\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+r\chi(X,{\mathcal{O}}_{X})+\sum_{x\in{\mathop{{\rm Sing\,}}}X}a(x,{\mathcal{E}}),

where the terms a⁡(x,ℰ)a(x,{\mathcal{E}}) depend only on the local reflexive modules at the singular points (see [Lan25, Theorem 4.4]). The main aim of this paper is to prove that for every closed point x∈Xx\in X there exists a constant CxC_{x} such that |a⁡(x,ℰ)|≤Cx​r|a(x,{\mathcal{E}})|\leq C_{x}r for all ℰ{\mathcal{E}}. This result was conjectured in [Lan00, Conjecture 8.2] (see also [Lan25, Remark 3.14]). It implies Wahl’s main conjecture [Wah93, Introduction] on the local asymptotic Riemann–Roch formula (see also [Lan00, Conjecture 4.1] and its generalization [Lan25, Conjecture 3.18]). As a corollary we obtain the following theorem improving [Lan25, Theorem 0.3].

Theorem 0.1.

Let XX be a normal proper algebraic surface defined over an algebraically closed field. Then there exists a constant CC depending only on XX such that for every rank rr coherent reflexive 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX we have

|χ(X,ℰ)−(12c1(ℰ).(c1(ℰ)−KX)−∫Xc2(ℰ)+rχ(X,𝒪X))|≤Cr.\left|\chi(X,{\mathcal{E}})-\left(\frac{1}{2}c_{1}({\mathcal{E}}).(c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})-K_{X})-\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+r\chi(X,{\mathcal{O}}_{X})\right)\right|\leq Cr.

We also prove that the Chern character of reflexive sheaves on a normal projective surface is a homomorphism of rings, as conjectured in [Lan25, Section 5.5] (see Theorem 3.1). More precisely, let Kref​(X)K^{{\mathop{\operatorname{\rm ref}}}}(X) be the Grothendieck ring of reflexive sheaves, with relations coming from locally split short exact sequences and multiplication given by reflexive tensor product. Then

ch:Kref​(X)⟶A∗​(X)⊗ℝ,[ℰ]⟼rkℰ+c1​(ℰ)+ch2(ℰ){\mathop{\rm ch\,}}:K^{{\mathop{\operatorname{\rm ref}}}}(X)\longrightarrow A^{*}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{R}},\qquad[{\mathcal{E}}]\longmapsto{\mathop{\rm rk\,}}{\mathcal{E}}+c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})+{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})

is a ring homomorphism, where the target has the ring structure induced by Mumford’s intersection product.

We use Theorem 0.1 to construct a good theory for the second Chern class (or character) for reflexive sheaves in higher dimensions. This was already done in [Lan25] in positive characteristic or for varieties with at most quotient singularities in codimension two in characteristic zero. Here we extend these results to arbitrary normal projective varieties and we prove the following theorem strengthening [Lan25, Theorem 0.4] (see Theorems 3.7 and 3.11).

Theorem 0.2.

For any normal projective variety XX of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field kk and for any coherent reflexive 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX there exists a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-multilinear symmetric form ∫Xc2​(ℰ):PicX×(n−2)→ℝ\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}):{\mathop{\rm Pic\,}}X^{\times(n-2)}\to{\mathbb{R}} such that:

  1. 1.

    If ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is a vector bundle on XX then

    ∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2=∫Xc2​(ℰ)∩c1​(L1)∩…∩c1​(Ln−2)∩[X].\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}=\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})\cap c_{1}(L_{1})\cap...\cap c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cap[X].
  2. 2.

    If k⊂Kk\subset K is an algebraically closed field extension then

    ∫XKc2​(ℰK)​(L1)K​…​(Ln−2)K=∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2.\int_{X_{K}}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}_{K})(L_{1})_{K}...(L_{n-2})_{K}=\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}.
  3. 3.

    If n>2n>2 and L1L_{1} is very ample then for a very general hypersurface H∈|L1|H\in|L_{1}| we have

    ∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2=∫Hc2​(ℰ|H)​L2|H​…​Ln−2|H.\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}=\int_{H}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}|_{H})L_{2}|_{H}...L_{n-2}|_{H}.
  4. 4.

    If π:Y→X\pi:Y\to X is a finite surjective morphism from a normal projective variety YY, then

    ∫Yc2​(π[∗]​ℰ)​π∗​L1​…​π∗​Ln−2=deg⁡π⋅∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2.\int_{Y}c_{2}(\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})\pi^{*}L_{1}...\pi^{*}L_{n-2}=\deg\pi\cdot\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}.

The second Chern class satisfies also the following asymptotic version of the Riemann–Roch theorem (see Proposition 3.5 and Definition 3.6).

Theorem 0.3.

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a rank rr coherent reflexive 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module on XX as above. Then for any line bundles L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},...,L_{n-2} on XX we have

χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅Sym[m]ℰ)\displaystyle\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\right)
=mr+1(r+1)!(c1(ℰ)2.L1…Ln−2−∫Xc2(ℰ)L1…Ln−2)+O(mr).\displaystyle\qquad=\frac{m^{r+1}}{(r+1)!}\left(c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})^{2}.L_{1}...L_{n-2}-\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}\right)+O(m^{r}).

We also prove the following characterization of the discriminant ∫XΔ⁡(ℰ)=2​r​∫Xc2​(ℰ)−(r−1)​c1​(ℰ)2\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})=2r\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})-(r-1)c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})^{2}:

Theorem 0.4.

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field, and let L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-2} be nef line bundles on XX. For every reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX we have

∫XΔ(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2=inff,ℱ∫ZΔ(ℱ)f∗L1⋯f∗Ln−2deg⁡f,\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}=\inf_{f,{\mathcal{F}}}\frac{\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})f^{*}L_{1}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-2}}{\deg f},

where f:Z→Xf:Z\to X runs through all alterations from smooth projective varieties, and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} runs through all vector bundles on ZZ satisfying g[∗]​ℱ≃h[∗]​ℰ,g_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}\simeq h^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}, with Z→𝑔Y→ℎXZ\xrightarrow{g}Y\xrightarrow{h}X the Stein factorization of ff.

The above theorem easily implies Bogomolov’s inequality for (strongly) slope semistable sheaves on normal projective varieties (see Corollary 4.9). This inequality implies a strong restriction theorem and boundedness results on normal projective varieties in characteristic zero (see Section 5). As a corollary we also prove a generalization of Miyaoka’s inequality on the second Chern class of the cotangent bundle of a smooth non-uniruled complex variety with nef KXK_{X} to normal projective varieties (see Corollary 5.11).

In the case of normal complex Kähler varieties a weaker form of Bogomolov’s inequality for slope semistable sheaves was proven by Chen in [Che25] (see Subsection 4.3).

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 1 we prove the uniform linear bound for the local Riemann–Roch correction terms. In Section 2 we establish the tensor and symmetric-power formulas for relative Chern characters and derive the local asymptotic Riemann–Roch formula. Section 3 studies the Chern character on normal surfaces and constructs second Chern classes in higher dimensions, proving their compatibility with finite pullbacks. In Section 4 we characterize discriminants by approximation with vector bundles on smooth alterations and compare our invariant with Chen’s. Section 5 contains applications to Bogomolov’s inequality, restriction theorems, boundedness, Miyaoka-type inequalities, and bigness of reflexive sheaves and finiteness of curves of low genus on normal surfaces. Finally, the appendix shows that in higher degrees the expected asymptotic Riemann–Roch formula is incompatible with the usual duality formula, already for rank-one reflexive sheaves.

Notation

We use the notation of [Lan25]. For a coherent sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on a normal scheme XX we write Sym[m]ℰ=(Symmℰ)∗⁣∗{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}=({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{m}{\mathcal{E}})^{**}. For coherent sheaves ℰ{\mathcal{E}} and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} we also write ℰ​⊗^​ℱ:=(ℰ⊗ℱ)∗⁣∗{\mathcal{E}}\hat{\otimes}{\mathcal{F}}:=({\mathcal{E}}\otimes{\mathcal{F}})^{**}. If f:X→Yf:X\to Y is a morphism of normal schemes, ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is a coherent sheaf on XX and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} a coherent sheaf on YY then we write f[∗]​ℱ=(f∗​ℱ)∗⁣∗f^{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}=(f^{*}{\mathcal{F}})^{**} and f[∗]​ℰ=(f∗​ℰ)∗⁣∗f_{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}=(f_{*}{\mathcal{E}})^{**}.

1 Local correction to the Riemann–Roch theorem

In this section we fix the following notation. Let kk be an algebraically closed field and let AA be the henselization of the local ring of a normal algebraic surface at a closed point. Put X=SpecAX={\mathop{{\rm Spec\,}}}A, and write xx for its closed point. We fix a projective good resolution f:X~→Xf:\tilde{X}\to X, which is an isomorphism over U=X\{x}U=X\backslash\{x\}. We write E=⋃i=1sEiE=\bigcup_{i=1}^{s}E_{i} for the reduced exceptional divisor. Its irreducible components are smooth projective curves, and its intersection matrix is negative definite.

1.1 Relative Chern classes and the correction term

Here we recall a few notions from [Lan00] and [Lan25] (see also [Wah93]).

For a vector bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} of rank rr on X~\tilde{X}, c1​(f,ℱ)c_{1}(f,{\mathcal{F}}) is the exceptional ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-divisor determined by

c1​(f,ℱ).Ei=deg⁡(ℱ|Ei).c_{1}(f,{\mathcal{F}}).E_{i}=\deg({\mathcal{F}}|_{E_{i}}).

We use the relative second Chern class c2​(f,ℱ)c_{2}(f,{\mathcal{F}}) from [Lan25, Definition 3.1]. More explicitly, let π~:Y~→X~\tilde{\pi}:\tilde{Y}\to\tilde{X} be a generically finite proper morphism from a regular surface, and let Y~→𝑔Y→X\tilde{Y}\xrightarrow{g}Y\to X be the Stein factorization of f​π~f\tilde{\pi}. For a filtration of π~∗​ℱ\tilde{\pi}^{*}{\mathcal{F}} with line bundle quotients ℒ1,…,ℒr{\mathcal{L}}_{1},...,{\mathcal{L}}_{r}, put Li=c1​(g,ℒi)L_{i}=c_{1}(g,{\mathcal{L}}_{i}). Then

c2​(f,ℱ)=inf∑i<jLi.Ljdeg⁡π~,c_{2}(f,{\mathcal{F}})=\inf\frac{\sum_{i<j}L_{i}.L_{j}}{\deg\tilde{\pi}},

where the infimum is taken over these morphisms and filtrations. We also set

ch2(f,ℱ):=12​c1​(f,ℱ)2−c2​(f,ℱ),Δ⁡(f,ℱ):=2​r​c2​(f,ℱ)−(r−1)​c1​(f,ℱ)2.{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}(f,{\mathcal{F}}):=\frac{1}{2}c_{1}(f,{\mathcal{F}})^{2}-c_{2}(f,{\mathcal{F}}),\quad\Delta(f,{\mathcal{F}}):=2rc_{2}(f,{\mathcal{F}})-(r-1)c_{1}(f,{\mathcal{F}})^{2}.

The relative Euler characteristic is defined by

χ⁡(f,ℱ)=dimH0​(X,f[∗]​ℱ/f∗​ℱ)+dimH0​(X,R1​f∗​ℱ).\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}})=\dim H^{0}(X,f_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}/f_{*}{\mathcal{F}})+\dim H^{0}(X,R^{1}f_{*}{\mathcal{F}}).

We also define the correction term to a local Riemann–Roch formula as

a⁡(f,ℱ):=χ⁡(f,ℱ)−r​χ​(f,𝒪X~)+12​c1​(f,ℱ).(c1​(f,ℱ)−KX~)−c2​(f,ℱ).a(f,{\mathcal{F}}):=\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}})-r\chi(f,{\mathcal{O}}_{\tilde{X}})+\frac{1}{2}c_{1}(f,{\mathcal{F}}).(c_{1}(f,{\mathcal{F}})-K_{\tilde{X}})-c_{2}(f,{\mathcal{F}}).

By [Lan25, Proposition 3.7], this number depends only on f[∗]​ℱf_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}. For a reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX, we denote it by a⁡(x,ℰ)a(x,{\mathcal{E}}). The main aim of this section is to prove the following bound on the correction terms a⁡(x,ℰ)a(x,{\mathcal{E}}).

Theorem 1.1.

There exists a constant CxC_{x} depending only on the germ (X,x)(X,x) such that for every coherent reflexive 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of rank rr we have

|a⁡(x,ℰ)|≤Cx​r.|a(x,{\mathcal{E}})|\leq C_{x}r.

The proof in characteristic zero uses vector bundles minimizing the relative Euler characteristic. Elementary transformations give bounds for the Harder–Narasimhan slopes of their restrictions to the exceptional curves. An induction on rank, using complete intersections in a projective bundle, converts these bounds into a relative discriminant estimate. We then construct finite covers using roots of a fixed collection of functions. The eigensheaves of these covers belong to a fixed finite collection of exceptional line bundles. This controls the geometric genera of the covering singularities and gives the required linear bound.

In positive characteristic the proof is easier and it uses the results of [Lan25] and a bound on the difference between a Frobenius pullback of a reflexive module and its reflexive hull.

1.2 Minimal extensions

Definition 1.2.

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a coherent reflexive 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module. We say that a vector bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on X~\tilde{X} is a minimal extension of ℰ{\mathcal{E}} if χ⁡(f,ℱ)\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}}) is minimal among the relative Euler characteristics of vector bundles with f[∗]​ℱ≃ℰf_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}\simeq{\mathcal{E}}.

Since χ⁡(f,ℱ)\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}}) is a non-negative integer, every reflexive sheaf on XX admits a minimal extension.

Lemma 1.3.

Let ℱ{\mathcal{F}} be a minimal extension of some reflexive sheaf. If CC is an irreducible component of EE of genus gg, then

g−1≤μmin​(ℱ|C)≤μmax​(ℱ|C)≤g−1−C2.g-1\leq\mu_{\min}({\mathcal{F}}|_{C})\leq\mu_{\max}({\mathcal{F}}|_{C})\leq g-1-C^{2}.
Proof.

Let ℱ|C→𝒬{\mathcal{F}}|_{C}\to{\mathcal{Q}} be the minimal destabilizing quotient and let ℱ′{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime} be the kernel of ℱ→i∗​𝒬{\mathcal{F}}\to i_{*}{\mathcal{Q}}, where i:C↪X~i:C\hookrightarrow\tilde{X}. The bundle ℱ′{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime} is locally free and agrees with ℱ{\mathcal{F}} off CC. Since their reflexive pushforwards are the same, the exact sequence gives

χ⁡(f,ℱ′)−χ⁡(f,ℱ)=χ⁡(C,𝒬).\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime})-\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}})=\chi(C,{\mathcal{Q}}).

Minimality implies that χ⁡(C,𝒬)≥0\chi(C,{\mathcal{Q}})\geq 0. Hence μmin​(ℱ|C)=μ⁡(𝒬)≥g−1\mu_{\min}({\mathcal{F}}|_{C})=\mu({\mathcal{Q}})\geq g-1.

Similarly, let 𝒮⊂ℱ|C{\mathcal{S}}\subset{\mathcal{F}}|_{C} be the maximal destabilizing subbundle. The elementary transformation

ℱ′′=ker⁡(ℱ⁡(C)⟶i∗​((ℱ|C/𝒮)⊗𝒪C​(C))){\mathcal{F}}^{\prime\prime}=\ker\bigl({\mathcal{F}}(C)\longrightarrow i_{*}(({\mathcal{F}}|_{C}/{\mathcal{S}})\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{C}(C))\bigr)

is locally free and fits into an exact sequence

0⟶ℱ⟶ℱ′′⟶i∗​(𝒮⁡(C))⟶0.0\longrightarrow{\mathcal{F}}\longrightarrow{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime\prime}\longrightarrow i_{*}({\mathcal{S}}(C))\longrightarrow 0.

Thus

χ⁡(f,ℱ′′)−χ⁡(f,ℱ)=−χ⁡(C,𝒮⁡(C))≥0,\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime\prime})-\chi(f,{\mathcal{F}})=-\chi(C,{\mathcal{S}}(C))\geq 0,

which gives μmax​(ℱ|C)=μ⁡(𝒮)≤g−1−C2\mu_{\max}({\mathcal{F}}|_{C})=\mu({\mathcal{S}})\leq g-1-C^{2}. ∎

ξ=c1​(𝒪ℙ⁡(ℱ)​(1)),η=ξ−1r​p∗​c1​(ℱ),B=η+2​p∗​T.\xi=c_{1}({\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{F}})}(1)),\qquad\eta=\xi-\frac{1}{r}p^{*}c_{1}({\mathcal{F}}),\qquad B=\eta+2p^{*}T.

μmin​(ℱ|Ei)−μ⁡(ℱ|Ei)+2​T​Ei≥T​Ei>0.\mu_{\min}({\mathcal{F}}|_{E_{i}})-\mu({\mathcal{F}}|_{E_{i}})+2TE_{i}\geq TE_{i}>0.

Consequently BB is ample relative to f​pfp. Choose a sufficiently large divisible integer mm so that m​BmB is an integral very ample class relative to XX, and intersect r−1r-1 general members of this linear system. Bertini’s theorem on each ℙ⁡(ℱ|Ei){\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{F}}|_{E_{i}}), together with transversality on the fibers over the nodes of EE, gives a surface Y~\tilde{Y} such that each

Ci=Y~∩p−1​(Ei)C_{i}=\tilde{Y}\cap p^{-1}(E_{i})

The morphism

π~=p|Y~:Y~⟶X~\tilde{\pi}=p|_{\tilde{Y}}:\tilde{Y}\longrightarrow\tilde{X}

is proper and generically finite of degree d=mr−1d=m^{r-1}, and each CiC_{i} dominates EiE_{i}. A positive-dimensional fiber over a point of EiE_{i} would contain a curve component of CiC_{i}, contradicting its irreducibility and dominance over EiE_{i}. Thus π~\tilde{\pi} is quasi-finite above EE. The locus in X~\tilde{X} over which its fibers have positive dimension is closed, and its image under ff is a closed subset of the local scheme XX not containing xx. It is therefore empty, so π~\tilde{\pi} is finite.

2 Properties of relative Chern characters

We keep the local notation from the preceding section. In particular, f:X~→Xf:\tilde{X}\to X is a resolution of an algebraic normal surface singularity, with exceptional divisor EE.

2.1 Discriminants of symmetric powers

In this subsection we prove that the relative discriminants of symmetric powers satisfy the usual formula holding for discriminants of symmetric powers of a vector bundle. In characteristic zero we use extensions with small normalized discriminants, whereas in positive characteristic we use Frobenius and boundedness of the relative discriminants of reflexive pullbacks of fixed rank.

Let us recall that for a rank rr vector bundle ℰ{\mathcal{E}}, we have

rm:=rkSymmℰ=(m+r−1r−1)r_{m}:={\mathop{\rm rk\,}}{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{m}{\mathcal{E}}=\binom{m+r-1}{r-1}

and the discriminant satisfies

Δ⁡(Symmℰ)rm=(m+rr+1)​Δ⁡(ℰ)r.\frac{\Delta({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{m}{\mathcal{E}})}{r_{m}}=\binom{m+r}{r+1}\frac{\Delta({\mathcal{E}})}{r}. (5)

Indeed, if x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r} are the Chern roots of ℰ{\mathcal{E}}, then Δ(ℰ)=−∑i<j(xi−xj)2.\Delta({\mathcal{E}})=-\sum_{i<j}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}. The roots of Symmℰ{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{m}{\mathcal{E}} are ∑iαi​xi\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}x_{i}, indexed by the non-negative integers αi\alpha_{i} satisfying ∑iαi=m\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}=m. The elementary identity

∑|α|=m(∑iαi​xi−mr​∑ixi)2=(m+rr+1)r​∑i<j(xi−xj)2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\left(\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}x_{i}-\frac{m}{r}\sum_{i}x_{i}\right)^{2}=\frac{\binom{m+r}{r+1}}{r}\sum_{i<j}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}

therefore gives (5).

3 Second Chern classes

3.1 The Chern character of reflexive sheaves on surfaces

Let XX be a normal proper surface over an algebraically closed field. As in [Lan25, Section 5.5], let Kref​(X)K^{{\mathop{\operatorname{\rm ref}}}}(X) denote the Grothendieck group of coherent reflexive sheaves, with relations coming from locally split short exact sequences. Reflexive tensor product makes Kref​(X)K^{{\mathop{\operatorname{\rm ref}}}}(X) a ring with unit [𝒪X][{\mathcal{O}}_{X}]. We equip A∗​(X)⊗ℝA^{*}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{R}} with the ring structure induced by Mumford’s intersection product.

Theorem 3.1.

The Chern character ch:Kref​(X)→A∗​(X)⊗ℝ{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}:K^{{\mathop{\operatorname{\rm ref}}}}(X)\to A^{*}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{R}} given by [ℰ]↦rkℰ+c1​(ℰ)+ch2(ℰ)[{\mathcal{E}}]\mapsto{\mathop{\rm rk\,}}{\mathcal{E}}+c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})+{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}) is a homomorphism of rings.

Proof.

Let ℰ,ℱ\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F} be reflexive sheaves of ranks r,sr,s, respectively, and choose a good resolution f:Y→Xf:Y\to X. In A0​(X)⊗ℝA_{0}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, the definitions give

ch2(ℰ)=f∗​ch2(f[∗]​ℰ)−∑x∈SingXch2(fx,f[∗]​ℰ)​[x],{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})=f_{*}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}(f^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})-\sum_{x\in{\mathop{{\rm Sing\,}}}X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}(f_{x},f^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})[x],

where fxf_{x} denotes the induced resolution of the local singularity at xx. We also have

f∗​(c1​(f[∗]​ℰ)​c1​(f[∗]​ℱ))=c1​(ℰ)​c1​(ℱ)+∑x∈SingXc1​(fx,f[∗]​ℰ)​c1​(fx,f[∗]​ℱ)​[x].f_{*}(c_{1}(f^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})c_{1}(f^{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}))=c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})c_{1}({\mathcal{F}})+\sum_{x\in{\mathop{{\rm Sing\,}}}X}c_{1}(f_{x},f^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})c_{1}(f_{x},f^{[*]}{\mathcal{F}})[x].

Apply the same formulas to ℱ{\mathcal{F}} and ℰ​⊗^​ℱ{\mathcal{E}}\hat{\otimes}{\mathcal{F}}, using f[∗]​ℱf^{[*]}{\mathcal{F}} and f[∗]​ℰ⊗f[∗]​ℱf^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}\otimes f^{[*]}{\mathcal{F}} as extensions. Ordinary multiplicativity on YY and Lemma 2.3 then give

ch2(ℰ​⊗^​ℱ)=s​ch2(ℰ)+r​ch2(ℱ)+c1​(ℰ)​c1​(ℱ){\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}\hat{\otimes}{\mathcal{F}})=s{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+r{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{F}})+c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})c_{1}({\mathcal{F}})

in A0​(X)⊗ℝA_{0}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{R}}.

Reflexive pullback of a locally split short exact sequence is a locally split short exact sequence of vector bundles on YY. Ordinary additivity on YY, together with Lemma 2.3, proves additivity of ch2{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2} for these sequences. The corresponding identities for rank and first Chern class are immediate. Thus ch{\mathop{\rm ch\,}} is well defined, additive and multiplicative, and ch([𝒪X])=1{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}([{\mathcal{O}}_{X}])=1. ∎

The following properties of Chern classes of reflexive sheaves on surfaces follow from the results of Section 2.

Corollary 3.2.

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a rank rr reflexive sheaf on XX. Then for every m≥1m\geq 1, we have

Δ⁡(Sym[m]ℰ)rm=(m+rr+1)​Δ⁡(ℰ)r\frac{\Delta({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})}{r_{m}}=\binom{m+r}{r+1}\frac{\Delta({\mathcal{E}})}{r}

in A0​(X)⊗ℝA_{0}(X)\otimes\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

Choose a resolution f:X~→Xf:\tilde{X}\to X and a vector bundle ℱ{\mathcal{F}} with f[∗]​ℱ≃ℰf_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}\simeq{\mathcal{E}}. Let EE be the exceptional locus of ff. The definitions of the surface Chern classes give

Δ⁡(ℰ)=f∗​Δ​(ℱ)−∑x∈f⁡(E)Δ⁡(fx,ℱ)​[x]\Delta({\mathcal{E}})=f_{*}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})-\sum_{x\in f(E)}\Delta(f_{x},{\mathcal{F}})[x]

in A0​(X)⊗ℝ.A_{0}(X)\otimes{\mathbb{R}}. Since f[∗]​Symmℱ≃Sym[m]ℰf_{[*]}{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{m}{\mathcal{F}}\simeq{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}, the same identity, together with (5) and Theorem 2.2, yields

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a rank rr reflexive sheaf on XX. Then we have

3.2 Second Chern classes in higher dimensions

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field kk. Below K⁡(X)K(X) denotes the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves, Kd​(X)K_{d}(X) is its subgroup generated by sheaves with support of dimension at most dd, and

ℱ↦c1​(L)⋅ℱ=ℱ−L−1⊗ℱ{\mathcal{F}}\mapsto c_{1}(L)\cdot{\mathcal{F}}={\mathcal{F}}-L^{-1}\otimes{\mathcal{F}}

is an additive endomorphism of K⁡(X)K(X).

The following standard lemma is implicitly contained in [Lan25].

Lemma 3.4.

Assume that n>2n>2. Let L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},...,L_{n-2} be very ample line bundles on XX, and let SKS_{K} be the geometric generic complete intersection in |L1|×…×|Ln−2||L_{1}|\times...\times|L_{n-2}|, where KK is an algebraic closure of the function field of this parameter space. Then SKS_{K} and all the successive intersections are normal and integral. For every coherent reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX, its restriction to each of these intersections is reflexive, and

(Sym[m]ℰ)SK=Sym[m](ℰSK)(m≥0).({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})_{S_{K}}={\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}({\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}})\qquad(m\geq 0).

Moreover,

χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅ℰ)=χ⁡(SK,ℰSK).\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathcal{E}}\right)=\chi(S_{K},{\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}}).
Proposition 3.5.

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a reflexive sheaf of rank rr on XX. For arbitrary line bundles L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},...,L_{n-2} there exists a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}} such that

χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅Sym[m]ℰ)=a​mr+1+O⁡(mr).\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\right)=am^{r+1}+O(m^{r}).
Proof.

The computation in [Lan25, Lemmas 1.6 and 1.7] gives

[Sym[m]ℰ]−(m+r−1r−1)⁡[𝒪X]−(m+r−1r)⁡([ℰ]−r⁡[𝒪X])∈Kn−2​(X).[{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}]-\binom{m+r-1}{r-1}[{\mathcal{O}}_{X}]-\binom{m+r-1}{r}\bigl([{\mathcal{E}}]-r[{\mathcal{O}}_{X}]\bigr)\in K_{n-2}(X).

Since every divisor operator lowers the support filtration by one, applying any n−1n-1 such operators, for fixed M1,…,Mn−1M_{1},...,M_{n-1} we have

χ⁡(X,c1​(M1)​…​c1​(Mn−1)⋅Sym[m]ℰ)=O⁡(mr).\chi\left(X,c_{1}(M_{1})...c_{1}(M_{n-1})\cdot{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\right)=O(m^{r}). (6)

Every line bundle LL can be written as A⊗B−1A\otimes B^{-1} with AA and BB very ample. The identity

c1​(L)=c1​(A)−c1​(B)+c1​(L)​c1​(B)c_{1}(L)=c_{1}(A)-c_{1}(B)+c_{1}(L)c_{1}(B)

and (6) express the Euler characteristic in the proposition as the difference of the corresponding expressions with LL replaced by AA and BB, up to an O⁡(mr)O(m^{r}) error. Applying this successively to each LiL_{i}, it is enough to prove the assertion when all the LiL_{i} are very ample. In this case Lemma 3.4 gives

χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅Sym[m]ℰ)=χ⁡(SK,Sym[m](ℰSK)),\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\right)=\chi\left(S_{K},{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}({\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}})\right),

and the assertion follows from Corollary 3.3. ∎

Definition 3.6.

For ℰ∈Ref(𝒪X){\mathcal{E}}\in{\mathop{\operatorname{Ref}\,}}({\mathcal{O}}_{X}) and line bundles L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},...,L_{n-2} we set

∫Xs2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2:=(r+1)!​limm→∞χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅Sym[m]ℰ)mr+1\int_{X}s_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}:=(r+1)!\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\right)}{m^{r+1}}

and

∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2:=c1​(ℰ)2.L1​…​Ln−2−∫Xs2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2,\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}:=c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})^{2}.L_{1}...L_{n-2}-\int_{X}s_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2},

where r=rk⁡ℰr=\operatorname{rk}\mathcal{E}. We also set

∫Xch2(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2:=12​c1​(ℰ)2.L1​…​Ln−2−∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2,\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}:=\frac{1}{2}c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})^{2}.L_{1}...L_{n-2}-\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2},

and define ∫XΔ⁡(ℰ)=2​r​∫Xc2​(ℰ)−(r−1)​c1​(ℰ)2\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})=2r\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})-(r-1)c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})^{2}.

Proposition 3.5 and the above definition imply that

χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅Sym[m]ℰ)=mr+1(r+1)!​∫Xs2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2+O⁡(mr).\displaystyle\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\right)=\frac{m^{r+1}}{(r+1)!}\int_{X}s_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}+O(m^{r}).
Theorem 3.7.

For each reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX, ∫Xc2​(ℰ):N1​(X)ℝ×(n−2)→ℝ\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}):N^{1}(X)_{{\mathbb{R}}}^{\times(n-2)}\to{\mathbb{R}} is a symmetric multilinear form with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    If XX is a surface, it is the degree of the second Chern class defined in [Lan25, Section 4.1].

  2. 2.

    If ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is locally free, then

    ∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2=∫Xc2​(ℰ)∩c1​(L1)∩…∩c1​(Ln−2)∩[X],\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}=\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})\cap c_{1}(L_{1})\cap...\cap c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cap[X],

    where the right hand side uses the ordinary Chern class of a vector bundle.

  3. 3.

    If k⊂Kk\subset K is an algebraically closed field extension, then

    ∫XKc2​(ℰK)​(L1)K​…​(Ln−2)K=∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2.\int_{X_{K}}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}_{K})(L_{1})_{K}...(L_{n-2})_{K}=\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}.
  4. 4.

    If n>2n>2 and L1L_{1} is very ample, then for a very general H∈|L1|H\in|L_{1}|,

    ∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2=∫Hc2​(ℰ|H)​(L2)|H​…​(Ln−2)|H.\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}=\int_{H}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}|_{H})(L_{2})|_{H}...(L_{n-2})|_{H}.

    In particular, if all LiL_{i} are very ample, then for a very general complete intersection surface SS,

    ∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2=∫Sc2​(ℰ|S).\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}=\int_{S}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}|_{S}).

These forms are uniquely determined by properties (1), (3) and (4).

Proof.

Proposition 3.5 and the identity

c1​(L⊗M)=c1​(L)+c1​(M)−c1​(L)​c1​(M),c_{1}(L\otimes M)=c_{1}(L)+c_{1}(M)-c_{1}(L)c_{1}(M),

together with (6), show that the normalized limit is additive in each line-bundle argument. It is symmetric because the divisor operators commute. Singular Riemann–Roch shows that the Euler-characteristic expressions depend only on the numerical classes of the line bundles. Together with the corresponding properties of Weil-divisor intersections, this gives the asserted symmetric multilinear form on N1​(X)ℝN^{1}(X)_{{\mathbb{R}}}.

Property (1) follows from Corollary 3.3. Property (3) follows from flat base change for reflexive symmetric powers and Euler characteristics, together with invariance of Weil-divisor intersections under extension of the ground field. Property (4) follows from Lemma 3.4, after spreading out the reflexive restrictions of the countably many symmetric powers and using Definition 3.6.

We now prove (2). In dimension two, it follows from (1) and compatibility of the surface Chern classes with ordinary Chern classes of vector bundles. In higher dimensions, by multilinearity and (3), we may assume that all LiL_{i} are very ample and that the ground field is uncountable. Choose a very general complete-intersection surface S∈|L1|∩⋯∩|Ln−2|S\in|L_{1}|\cap\cdots\cap|L_{n-2}|. By (4), the surface case, and the projection formula, we have

∫Xc2(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2\displaystyle\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2} =∫Sc2​(ℰ|S)∩[S]\displaystyle=\int_{S}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}|_{S})\cap[S]
=∫Xc2​(ℰ)∩c1​(L1)∩⋯∩c1​(Ln−2)∩[X],\displaystyle=\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})\cap c_{1}(L_{1})\cap\cdots\cap c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cap[X],

where the right-hand sides use ordinary Chern classes. This proves (2).

Finally, properties (1), (3), and (4) determine the values on very ample tuples by restriction to a complete-intersection surface. Multilinearity then determines all values, since every line bundle is the difference of two very ample line bundles. ∎

Proposition 3.8.

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} be coherent reflexive sheaves of ranks rr and ss on a normal projective variety XX over an algebraically closed field. Then

∫Xch2(ℰ⊕ℱ)=∫Xch2(ℰ)+∫Xch2(ℱ)\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}\oplus{\mathcal{F}})=\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{F}})

and

∫Xch2(ℰ​⊗^​ℱ)=s​∫Xch2(ℰ)+r​∫Xch2(ℱ)+c1​(ℰ)​c1​(ℱ).\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}\hat{\otimes}{\mathcal{F}})=s\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+r\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{F}})+c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})c_{1}({\mathcal{F}}).
Proof.

By properties (1), (3) and (4) of Theorem 3.7 and multilinearity, it is enough to prove the identities on a normal projective surface. In this case the equalities follow from Theorem 3.1. ∎

Remark 3.9.

The above proposition and Corollary 3.2 extend to computations of the second Chern character of the reflexive sheaf associated to a given rank rr reflexive sheaf by some rational GLr\mathrm{GL}_{r}-representation.

3.3 The Riemann–Roch inequality on normal varieties

Theorem 3.10.

Let XX be a normal proper algebraic variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field. Let L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},...,L_{n-2} be very ample line bundles on XX. There is a constant CXC_{X} depending only on X,L1,…,Ln−2X,L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-2} such that for every reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of rank rr one has

|χ(X,c1(L1)…c1(Ln−2)⋅ℰ)\displaystyle\Big|\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathcal{E}}\right) −r​χ​(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅𝒪X)−∫Xch2(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2\displaystyle-r\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathcal{O}}_{X}\right)-\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}
+12c1(ℰ).(KX+L1+…+Ln−2).L1…Ln−2|≤CXr.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}c_{1}({\mathcal{E}}).(K_{X}+L_{1}+...+L_{n-2}).L_{1}...L_{n-2}\Big|\leq C_{X}r.
Proof.

If n=2n=2 then [Lan25, Theorem 4.4] implies that

|χ(X,ℰ)−rχ(X,𝒪X)−∫Xch2(ℰ)+12c1(ℰ).KX|=|∑x∈SingXa(x,ℰ)|.\displaystyle\left|\chi(X,{\mathcal{E}})-r\chi(X,{\mathcal{O}}_{X})-\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+\frac{1}{2}c_{1}({\mathcal{E}}).K_{X}\right|=\left|\sum_{x\in{\mathop{{\rm Sing\,}}}X}a(x,{\mathcal{E}})\right|.

So the assertion follows from Theorem 1.1.

If n>2n>2, let SKS_{K} be the fixed geometric generic surface from Lemma 3.4. For every reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX, that lemma gives reflexivity of ℰSK{\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}} and identifies the Euler characteristics in the assertion with those of ℰSK{\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}} and 𝒪SK{\mathcal{O}}_{S_{K}}. By Theorem 3.7,

∫Xch2(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2=∫SKch2(ℰSK).\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}=\int_{S_{K}}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}}).

Moreover, the canonical divisor of SKS_{K} is the restriction of KX+L1+…+Ln−2K_{X}+L_{1}+...+L_{n-2}. Thus the expression inside the absolute value is

∑x∈SingSKa⁡(x,ℰSK),\sum_{x\in{\mathop{{\rm Sing\,}}}S_{K}}a(x,{\mathcal{E}}_{S_{K}}),

and the assertion follows from Theorem 1.1. ∎

3.4 Chern classes of pullbacks by finite morphisms

Theorem 3.11.

If π:Y→X\pi:Y\to X is a finite surjective morphism from a normal projective variety, then for each reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX we have

∫Yc2​(π[∗]​ℰ)​π∗​L1​…​π∗​Ln−2=deg⁡π⋅∫Xc2​(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2\int_{Y}c_{2}(\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})\pi^{*}L_{1}...\pi^{*}L_{n-2}=\deg\pi\cdot\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}

for arbitrary line bundles L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-2} on XX.

Proof.

Assume first that kk has characteristic zero and all LiL_{i} are very ample. After extending the base field, let SS be the geometric generic complete intersection in |L1|×…×|Ln−2||L_{1}|\times...\times|L_{n-2}|, and put T=π−1​(S)T=\pi^{-1}(S). By Bertini’s theorem, TT is a normal surface. The incidence and Koszul arguments in the proof of Lemma 3.4 also apply to the pulled-back basepoint-free linear systems on YY. Thus all the reflexive symmetric powers under consideration restrict reflexively, and Definition 3.6 identifies the required Chern numbers with those on SS and TT. Moreover, (π[∗]​ℰ)|T≃(π|T)[∗]​(ℰ|S)(\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})|_{T}\simeq(\pi|_{T})^{[*]}({\mathcal{E}}|_{S}), because this equality holds away from finitely many points and both sides are reflexive. The finite morphism π|T:T→S\pi|_{T}:T\to S has degree deg⁡π\deg\pi, so [Lan25, Proposition 4.2] implies that

∫Tc2​((π[∗]​ℰ)|T)=deg⁡π⋅∫Sc2​(ℰ|S),\int_{T}c_{2}((\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})|_{T})=\deg\pi\cdot\int_{S}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}}|_{S}),

as required. Multilinearity gives the assertion for arbitrary line bundles.

Assume now that kk has characteristic p>0p>0. By restriction to a geometric generic complete-intersection surface, Theorem 3.7 and the surface Frobenius formula [Lan25, Proposition 4.2] give

∫Xch2(FX[e]​ℰ)=p2​e​∫Xch2(ℰ).\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}(F_{X}^{[e]}{\mathcal{E}})=p^{2e}\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}). (7)

The same equality holds for reflexive sheaves on YY.

By multilinearity, it is enough to prove the required equality when both LiL_{i} and π∗​Li\pi^{*}L_{i} are very ample: every line bundle is a difference of ample line bundles, and sufficiently large powers of an ample line bundle and its finite pullback are very ample. Put d=deg⁡πd=\deg\pi, r=rkℰr={\mathop{\rm rk\,}}{\mathcal{E}}, and 𝒜=π∗​𝒪Y{\mathcal{A}}=\pi_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}. For e≥0e\geq 0, put q=peq=p^{e} and ℬe=FX[e]​ℰ​⊗^​𝒜.{\mathcal{B}}_{e}=F_{X}^{[e]}{\mathcal{E}}\hat{\otimes}{\mathcal{A}}. We have a natural isomorphism ℬe≃π∗​FY[e]​(π[∗]​ℰ),{\mathcal{B}}_{e}\simeq\pi_{*}F_{Y}^{[e]}(\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}), as both sides are reflexive and agree on the big open subset of XX where ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is locally free.

The sheaf ℬe{\mathcal{B}}_{e} has rank r​drd and c1​(ℬe)=d​q​c1​(ℰ)+r​c1​(𝒜).c_{1}({\mathcal{B}}_{e})=dq\,c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})+r\,c_{1}({\mathcal{A}}). Moreover, Proposition 3.8 and (7) imply that

∫Xch2(ℬe)=d​q2​∫Xch2(ℰ)+q​c1​(ℰ)​c1​(𝒜)+r​∫Xch2(𝒜).\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{B}}_{e})=dq^{2}\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})+q\,c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})c_{1}({\mathcal{A}})+r\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{A}}).

Applying Theorem 3.10 to ℬe{\mathcal{B}}_{e}, we obtain

χ⁡(X,c1​(L1)​…​c1​(Ln−2)⋅ℬe)\displaystyle\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{1})...c_{1}(L_{n-2})\cdot{\mathcal{B}}_{e}\right) =∫Xch2(ℬe)​L1​…​Ln−2+O⁡(q)\displaystyle=\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{B}}_{e})L_{1}...L_{n-2}+O(q)
=d​q2​∫Xch2(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2+O⁡(q).\displaystyle=dq^{2}\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}+O(q).

Here the rank is fixed and the first-Chern-class term is O⁡(q)O(q). Similarly, applying Theorem 3.10 on YY gives

Since π\pi is finite, the two Euler characteristics agree by the projection formula. Dividing by q2q^{2} and letting e→∞e\to\infty, we obtain

∫Ych2(π[∗]​ℰ)​π∗​L1​…​π∗​Ln−2=d​∫Xch2(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2.\int_{Y}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}(\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})\pi^{*}L_{1}...\pi^{*}L_{n-2}=d\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}. (8)

c1​(π[∗]​ℰ)2.π∗​L1​…​π∗​Ln−2=d​c1​(ℰ)2.L1​…​Ln−2.c_{1}(\pi^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})^{2}.\pi^{*}L_{1}...\pi^{*}L_{n-2}=d\,c_{1}({\mathcal{E}})^{2}.L_{1}...L_{n-2}.

Together with (8), this proves the assertion. ∎

4 Approximation of discriminants by alterations

Definition 4.1.

Let XX be a normal projective variety over an algebraically closed field kk and let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a reflexive sheaf on XX. Let f:Z→Xf:Z\to X be an alteration from a smooth projective variety ZZ. We say that a reflexive sheaf ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on ZZ is compatible with ℰ{\mathcal{E}} if g[∗]​ℱ≃h[∗]​ℰ,g_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}\simeq h^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}, where Z→𝑔Y→ℎXZ\xrightarrow{g}Y\xrightarrow{h}X is the Stein factorization of ff. In this case we say that (f,ℱ)(f,{\mathcal{F}}) is compatible with (X,ℰ)(X,{\mathcal{E}}).

4.1 Approximation of discriminants on surfaces

Proposition 4.2.

The displayed isomorphism over XregX_{\rm reg} is stronger than compatibility, that is, gi⁡[∗]​ℱi≃πi[∗]​ℰg_{i[*]}{\mathcal{F}}_{i}\simeq\pi_{i}^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}. It does not imply that ℱi≃(f​π~i)[∗]​ℰ{\mathcal{F}}_{i}\simeq(f\widetilde{\pi}_{i})^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}}.

Corollary 4.4.

Let XX be a normal projective surface over an algebraically closed field. For every reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} on XX of positive rank, we have

∫XΔ⁡(ℰ)=inff,ℱ∫ZΔ⁡(ℱ)deg⁡f,\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})=\inf_{f,{\mathcal{F}}}\frac{\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})}{\deg f},

where f:Z→Xf:Z\to X runs through all alterations from smooth projective surfaces, and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} runs through all vector bundles on ZZ that are compatible with ℰ{\mathcal{E}}.

Proof.

Let (f,ℱ)(f,{\mathcal{F}}) be a pair compatible with (X,ℰ)(X,{\mathcal{E}}) and let Z→𝑔Y→ℎXZ\xrightarrow{g}Y\xrightarrow{h}X be the Stein factorization of ff. The birational discriminant inequality and finite-pullback functoriality give

∫ZΔ⁡(ℱ)≥∫YΔ⁡(g[∗]​ℱ)=∫YΔ⁡(h[∗]​ℰ)=(deg⁡f)​∫XΔ⁡(ℰ).\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})\geq\int_{Y}\Delta(g_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}})=\int_{Y}\Delta(h^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})=(\deg f)\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}}).

The reverse inequality follows from the approximating sequence in Proposition 4.2. ∎

Example 4.5.

The finite coverings cannot in general be omitted from the infimum. Let X=ℙ⁡(1,1,2)X={\mathbb{P}}(1,1,2), the projective quadric cone, let ℒ=𝒪X​(1){\mathcal{L}}={\mathcal{O}}_{X}(1), and put ℰ=𝒪X⊕ℒ{\mathcal{E}}={\mathcal{O}}_{X}\oplus{\mathcal{L}}. Then c1​(ℒ)2=1/2c_{1}({\mathcal{L}})^{2}=1/2, and hence ∫XΔ(ℰ)=−1/2.\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})=-1/2. For every vector bundle extension ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on a smooth resolution of XX, the ordinary discriminant is an integer and it is at least −1/2-1/2 by the local discriminant formula. It is therefore nonnegative. On the minimal resolution 𝔽2→X\mathbb{F}_{2}\to X, the bundle 𝒪𝔽2⊕𝒪𝔽2​(F){\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}\oplus{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(F), where FF is a fiber of the ruling, extends ℰ{\mathcal{E}} and has discriminant zero. Thus the infimum over resolutions of XX itself is zero, whereas the normalized infimum allowing finite covers is −1/2-1/2.

4.2 Approximation of discriminants in higher dimensions

The following lemma generalizes [Lan25, Proposition 4.2, (3)] to higher dimensions.

Lemma 4.6.

Let g:Z→Yg:Z\to Y be a projective birational morphism from a smooth projective variety to a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2. Let ℱ{\mathcal{F}} be a vector bundle on ZZ. Then for any nef line bundles H1,…,Hn−2H_{1},\ldots,H_{n-2} on YY we have

∫ZΔ(ℱ)g∗H1⋯g∗Hn−2≥∫YΔ(g[∗]ℱ)H1⋯Hn−2.\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})g^{*}H_{1}\cdots g^{*}H_{n-2}\geq\int_{Y}\Delta(g_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}})H_{1}\cdots H_{n-2}.
Proof.

Let us set 𝒢:=g[∗]​ℱ{\mathcal{G}}:=g_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}} and assume that all HiH_{i} are ample. Replacing them by sufficiently large multiples and extending the ground field if necessary, choose a sufficiently general normal complete-intersection surface S∈|H1|∩⋯∩|Hn−2|S\in|H_{1}|\cap\cdots\cap|H_{n-2}| such that 𝒢|S{\mathcal{G}}|_{S} is reflexive and the restriction formula for its discriminant holds.

We can also arrange that SS avoids the locus over which gg has fibers of dimension at least two. Indeed, this locus has codimension at least three: its inverse image is contained in the exceptional locus of gg, which has dimension at most n−1n-1. The nonisomorphism locus of gg meets SS in finitely many points.

Set W=g−1​(S)W=g^{-1}(S). Every irreducible component of WW has dimension at least two, whereas every fiber over the exceptional points of SS has dimension at most one. Thus WW has a unique irreducible component, dominating SS, and has dimension two. It is a complete intersection in the smooth variety ZZ, hence Cohen–Macaulay, and it is generically reduced because gg is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of SS. Consequently, WW is integral.

Let ρ:T→W\rho:T\to W be a resolution of its normalization and put 𝒱=ρ∗​(ℱ|W){\mathcal{V}}=\rho^{*}({\mathcal{F}}|_{W}). The induced morphism T→ST\to S is birational, and the reflexive direct image of 𝒱{\mathcal{V}} is 𝒢|S{\mathcal{G}}|_{S}. The projection formula and the surface discriminant inequality therefore give

∫ZΔ(ℱ)g∗H1⋯g∗Hn−2\displaystyle\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})g^{*}H_{1}\cdots g^{*}H_{n-2} =∫WΔ⁡(ℱ|W)=∫TΔ⁡(𝒱)\displaystyle=\int_{W}\Delta({\mathcal{F}}|_{W})=\int_{T}\Delta({\mathcal{V}})
≥∫SΔ(𝒢|S)=∫YΔ(𝒢)H1⋯Hn−2.\displaystyle\geq\int_{S}\Delta({\mathcal{G}}|_{S})=\int_{Y}\Delta({\mathcal{G}})H_{1}\cdots H_{n-2}.

This proves the assertion for ample line bundles. The nef case follows by continuity. ∎

The following theorem is a higher dimensional version of Corollary 4.4. We use alterations of general complete intersection surfaces coming from this corollary to reduce the higher dimensional version to the surface case.

Theorem 4.7.

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field, and let L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-2} be nef line bundles on XX. For every reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of positive rank on XX, we have

∫XΔ(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2=inff,ℱ∫ZΔ(ℱ)f∗L1⋯f∗Ln−2deg⁡f,\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}=\inf_{f,{\mathcal{F}}}\frac{\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})f^{*}L_{1}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-2}}{\deg f},

where f:Z→Xf:Z\to X runs through all alterations from smooth projective varieties, and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} runs through all vector bundles on ZZ compatible with ℰ{\mathcal{E}}.

Proof.

Let (f,ℱ)(f,{\mathcal{F}}) be compatible with (X,ℰ)(X,{\mathcal{E}}), and let Z→𝑔Y→ℎXZ\xrightarrow{g}Y\xrightarrow{h}X be the Stein factorization of ff. By Lemma 4.6 and Theorem 3.11 we have

∫ZΔ(ℱ)f∗L1⋯f∗Ln−2\displaystyle\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})f^{*}L_{1}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-2} ≥∫YΔ(h[∗]ℰ)h∗L1⋯h∗Ln−2\displaystyle\geq\int_{Y}\Delta(h^{[*]}{\mathcal{E}})h^{*}L_{1}\cdots h^{*}L_{n-2}
=(degf)∫XΔ(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2.\displaystyle=(\deg f)\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}.

This proves the required lower bound.

If n=2n=2, the opposite inequality follows from Corollary 4.4. Assume that n≥3n\geq 3. By extension of the algebraically closed ground field and specialization of the resulting alterations and bundles, we may assume that the ground field is uncountable.

Choose a sufficiently ample line bundle HH so that H⊗Li−1H\otimes L_{i}^{-1} is nef for every ii. For each compatible pair, the difference

∫ZΔ(ℱ)f∗L1⋯f∗Ln−2deg⁡f−∫XΔ(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2\frac{\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})f^{*}L_{1}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-2}}{\deg f}-\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}

is multilinear in the LiL_{i} and nonnegative on nef tuples. It therefore does not decrease when any LiL_{i} is replaced by HH. Hence it suffices to prove the assertion when L1=⋯=Ln−2=HL_{1}=\cdots=L_{n-2}=H.

Let U⊂XU\subset X be the open subset where XX is smooth and ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is locally free. Its complement has codimension at least two. Choose n−1n-1 very general sections of HH whose common zero locus is a smooth curve C⊂UC\subset U. They define a rational map X⇢ℙn−2X\dashrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{n-2}, which is resolved by the blowup q:P=BlC⁡X⟶X.q:P=\operatorname{Bl}_{C}X\longrightarrow X. Let λ:P→ℙn−2\lambda:P\to{\mathbb{P}}^{n-2} be the induced morphism and EE the exceptional divisor. Then

q∗​H=λ∗​𝒪ℙn−2​(1)+E.q^{*}H=\lambda^{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{n-2}}(1)+E. (9)

∫SΔ⁡(ℰ|S)=∫XΔ⁡(ℰ)​Hn−2.\int_{S}\Delta({\mathcal{E}}|_{S})=\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})H^{n-2}.

Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. By Proposition 4.2, there exist an alteration aη:V→Sa_{\eta}:V\to S and a vector bundle 𝒱{\mathcal{V}} on VV such that

Over a dense open subset of ℙn−2{\mathbb{P}}^{n-2}, the descended bundle and its isomorphism with the pullback of ℰ{\mathcal{E}} over UU extend. a=w​β​t,f=q​a,ℱ=t∗​𝒱′.a=w\beta t,\qquad f=qa,\qquad{\mathcal{F}}=t^{*}{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime}.

Remark 4.8.

The nef hypothesis in Theorem 4.7 cannot be replaced by arbitrary Cartier divisors. For example, let g:Z→Xg:Z\to X be the blowup of a smooth projective threefold XX along a smooth curve C⊂XC\subset X, with exceptional divisor EE, and let LL be a Cartier divisor on XX. Set ℰ=𝒪X⊕2\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{O}_{X}^{\oplus 2} and ℱt=𝒪Z​(t​E)⊕𝒪Z​(−t​E).\mathcal{F}_{t}=\mathcal{O}_{Z}(tE)\oplus\mathcal{O}_{Z}(-tE). Then g[∗]​ℱt≃ℰg_{[*]}\mathcal{F}_{t}\simeq\mathcal{E} but

∫ZΔ⁡(ℱt)​g∗​L=4​t2​(L⋅C).\int_{Z}\Delta(\mathcal{F}_{t})g^{*}L=4t^{2}(L\cdot C).

If L⋅C<0L\cdot C<0, the infimum is −∞-\infty, whereas the discriminant of ℰ\mathcal{E} is zero.

Corollary 4.9.

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field, and let L=(L1,…,Ln−1)L=(L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-1}) be a collection of nef line bundles on XX such that the 11-cycle L1​…​Ln−1L_{1}\ldots L_{n-1} is numerically non-trivial. If ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is a strongly slope LL-semistable reflexive sheaf then

∫XΔ⁡(ℰ)​L2​…​Ln−1≥0.\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\dots L_{n-1}\geq 0.

Let (f,ℱ)(f,{\mathcal{F}}) be a pair compatible with (X,ℰ)(X,{\mathcal{E}}). Then ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is strongly (f∗​L1,…,f∗​Ln−1)(f^{*}L_{1},\ldots,f^{*}L_{n-1})-semistable and Bogomolov’s inequality on ZZ (see [Lan04b, Theorem 3.4]) gives

∫ZΔ(ℱ)f∗L2⋯f∗Ln−1≥0.\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})f^{*}L_{2}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-1}\geq 0.

So the inequality follows from Theorem 4.7. ∎

4.3 Relation to Chen’s results

Let XX be a normal complex projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2, and let L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-2} be ample line bundles. In this setting, Chen in [Che25] defined the discriminant of a reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} as

∫XΔChen(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2=inff,ℱ∫ZΔ(ℱ)f∗L1⋯f∗Ln−2,\int_{X}\Delta_{\mathrm{Chen}}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}=\inf_{f,{\mathcal{F}}}\int_{Z}\Delta({\mathcal{F}})f^{*}L_{1}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-2},

where f:Z→Xf:Z\to X runs through projective birational morphisms from smooth projective varieties, and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} runs through reflexive sheaves satisfying f[∗]​ℱ≃ℰf_{[*]}{\mathcal{F}}\simeq{\mathcal{E}}. His definition used analytic sheaves and Kähler resolutions but a compact Kähler resolution of a projective variety is projective, and GAGA identifies its coherent analytic sheaves with algebraic ones. So the above formula gives the invariant defined in [Che25].

Note that the infimum is unchanged if we restrict to vector bundles. So by Theorem 4.7, we have

∫XΔChen(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2≥∫XΔ(ℰ)L1⋯Ln−2.\int_{X}\Delta_{\mathrm{Chen}}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}\geq\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}.

This inequality can be strict, as shown by Example 4.5.

Suppose now that ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is slope semistable with respect to a collection of ample line bundles (L1,…,Ln−1)(L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-1}). In this case Chen also proved a Bogomolov type inequality (see [Che25, Theorem 1.14]). His inequality follows immediately from Bogomolov’s inequality on the resolutions of XX (as in the proof of Corollary 4.9) and it is usually weaker than that in Corollary 4.9. The non-trivial part of [Che25, Theorem 1.14] is the second one that concerns equality ∫XΔChen(ℰ)L2⋯Ln−1=0\int_{X}\Delta_{\mathrm{Chen}}({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0. Then [Che25, Theorem 1.14] gives a filtration with torsion-free quotients whose restrictions to XregX_{\rm reg} are projectively unitary flat. Corollary 4.9 implies that in this case ∫XΔ(ℰ)L2⋯Ln−1=0.\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0.

We expect the following stronger statement. If ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is slope polystable with respect to (L1,…,Ln−1)(L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-1}) and

∫XΔ(ℰ)L2⋯Ln−1=0,\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0,

then ℰ|Xreg{\mathcal{E}}|_{X_{\rm reg}} is locally free and projectively unitary flat. More precisely, writing r=rkℰr={\mathop{\rm rk\,}}{\mathcal{E}}, we expect that the analytic projectivization of ℰ|Xreg{\mathcal{E}}|_{X_{\rm reg}} is induced by a representation π1​(Xregan)→PU⁡(r).\pi_{1}(X_{\rm reg}^{\rm an})\to\operatorname{PU}(r). This conclusion does not follow from the comparison above, since vanishing of our discriminant does not imply vanishing of Chen’s invariant.

Conversely, projective unitary flatness of ℰ|Xreg{\mathcal{E}}|_{X_{\rm reg}} implies the asserted discriminant vanishing. Let us set 𝒜=ℰ​⊗^​ℰ∗{\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{E}}\hat{\otimes}{\mathcal{E}}^{*}. Then 𝒜|Xreg{\mathcal{A}}|_{X_{\rm reg}} is unitary flat and ∫Xch2(𝒜)=−∫XΔ(ℰ).\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{A}})=-\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}}). So applying [Lan26, Lemma 6.12] to the restriction of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} to a very general normal complete-intersection surface gives

∫XΔ(ℰ)L2⋯Ln−1=−∫Xch2(𝒜)L2⋯Ln−1=0.\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=-\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{A}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0.

For more details and an interpretation of vanishing of the discriminant in the semistable case, we refer to [Lan26, Sections 5 and 6].

5 Applications

In this section we prove strong restriction theorems for semistable sheaves on normal varieties and we show some new boundedness results in characteristic zero. We also prove a Miyaoka type inequality and some hyperbolicity results on normal surfaces.

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension nn defined over an algebraically closed field kk and let L=(L1,…,Ln−1)L=(L_{1},...,L_{n-1}) be a collection of nef line bundles on XX such that the 11-cycle L1​…​Ln−1L_{1}...L_{n-1} is numerically nontrivial. Let us first note the following generalization of [Lan24, Lemma 2.1]:

Lemma 5.1.

Let

0→ℰ1→ℰ→ℰ20\to{\mathcal{E}}_{1}\to{\mathcal{E}}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{2}

be an exact sequence of reflexive sheaves on XX and assume that the cokernel of the last map is supported in codimension ≥2\geq 2. Then we have

∫Xch2(ℰ)​L1​…​Ln−2≤∫Xch2(ℰ1)​L1​…​Ln−2+∫Xch2(ℰ2)​L1​…​Ln−2.\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{1}...L_{n-2}\leq\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}_{1})L_{1}...L_{n-2}+\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}({\mathcal{E}}_{2})L_{1}...L_{n-2}.

Moreover, if the last map in the above sequence is surjective and the sequence is locally split in codimension 22 then in the above inequality we have equality.

Proof.

If kk has positive characteristic then the assertion follows from [Lan24, Lemma 2.1]. So we can assume that kk has characteristic 00. In case XX is a surface, the above inequality was proven in [Lan26, Lemma 1.2]. So the inequality follows from Theorem 3.7 as in the proof of [Lan24, Lemma 2.1]. For the last assertion, restrict to a geometric generic complete-intersection surface. Then the sequence becomes locally split everywhere, so Theorem 3.1 gives additivity. ∎

Let us note that [Lan24, Lemma 2.3] holds also in characteristic zero:

Lemma 5.6.

Let H∈|L1|H\in|L_{1}| be a normal integral divisor and let i:H↪Xi:H\hookrightarrow X denote the closed embedding. Let TT be a torsion free coherent 𝒪H{\mathcal{O}}_{H}-module of rank τ\tau and let

be a short exact sequence of coherent 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-modules, where ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is reflexive of rank rr. Then 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is reflexive and

∫XΔ⁡(𝒢)​L2​…​Ln−1=\displaystyle\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{G}})L_{2}...L_{n-1}={} ∫XΔ⁡(ℰ)​L2​…​Ln−1−τ⁡(r−τ)​L12​L2​…​Ln−1\displaystyle\int_{X}\Delta({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}...L_{n-1}-\tau(r-\tau)L_{1}^{2}L_{2}...L_{n-1}

=−τ⁡(r−τ)​H2+2​(r​degH​T−τ​degH⁡(i∗​ℰ)),\displaystyle=-\tau(r-\tau)H^{2}+2\bigl(r\deg_{H}T-\tau\deg_{H}(i^{*}{\mathcal{E}})\bigr),

5.3 A Miyaoka-type inequality

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field kk. For a collection L=(L1,…,Ln−1)L=(L_{1},...,L_{n-1}) of nef line bundles (or just nef ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Cartier ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisors) on XX we set

Lmin,L​(ℰ)={μmin,L​(ℰ),if ​char⁡k=0,lime→∞μmin,L​(FX[e]​ℰ)pe,if ​char⁡k=p>0,L_{\min,L}({\mathcal{E}})=\begin{cases}\mu_{\min,L}({\mathcal{E}}),&\text{if }\operatorname{char}k=0,\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\lim_{e\to\infty}\frac{\mu_{\min,L}(F_{X}^{[e]}{\mathcal{E}})}{p^{e}},&\text{if }\operatorname{char}k=p>0,\end{cases}

where FX[e]​ℰ=((FXe)∗​ℰ)∗⁣∗F_{X}^{[e]}{\mathcal{E}}=((F_{X}^{e})^{*}{\mathcal{E}})^{**}. We say that a coherent reflexive sheaf ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is generically LL-semipositive if Lmin,L​(ℰ)≥0L_{\min,L}({\mathcal{E}})\geq 0. We say that ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is generically semipositive if it is generically LL-semipositive for every collection LL of ample divisors.

The following result extends Miyaoka’s theorem [Miy87, Theorem 6.1] (see also [Lan15, Theorems 9.2 and 9.3] for the positive characteristic versions) to reflexive sheaves on normal varieties.

Theorem 5.10.

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a coherent reflexive sheaf on XX, and assume that L1=c1​(ℰ)L_{1}=c_{1}({\mathcal{E}}) is a nef ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-Cartier divisor. Fix nef line bundles L2,…,Ln−1L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1}. Assume that one of the following conditions holds:

  1. 1.

    The 11-cycle L1⋯Ln−1L_{1}\cdots L_{n-1} is numerically non-trivial and ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is generically (L1,…,Ln−1)(L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-1})-semipositive.

  2. 2.

    The 11-cycle L1⋯Ln−1L_{1}\cdots L_{n-1} is numerically trivial and ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is generically (A,L2,…,Ln−1)(A,L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1})-semipositive for some ample Cartier divisor AA.

Then

∫Xc2(ℰ)L2⋯Ln−1≥0.\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}\geq 0.

In particular, if ℰ\mathcal{E} is generically semipositive and c1​(ℰ)c_{1}(\mathcal{E}) is nef and ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Cartier, then the inequality holds for every collection of nef line bundles L2,…,Ln−1L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1}.

Proof.

The numerical argument of [Lan15, Lemma 9.1] applies to filtrations of reflexive sheaves with torsion free quotients, after replacing the quotients by their reflexive hulls. Indeed, Lemma 5.1 supplies the required inequality for ch2{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{2}, and the Hodge index theorem applies to Weil-divisor intersections.

In case (1), the proof of [Lan15, Theorem 9.2] therefore applies, using Corollary 4.9 and the ordinary Harder–Narasimhan filtration in characteristic zero and the strong Harder–Narasimhan filtration of a reflexive Frobenius pullback in positive characteristic. In positive characteristic we also use Frobenius functoriality of the second Chern class.

Consider case (2). Since μ(A,L2,…,Ln−1)​(ℰ)=0\mu_{(A,L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1})}({\mathcal{E}})=0, generic semipositivity implies that ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is strongly (A,L2,…,Ln−1)(A,L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1})-semistable. Hence if A.L2⋯Ln−1A.L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1} is numerically non-trivial, then Corollary 4.9 gives

2r∫Xc2(ℰ)L2⋯Ln−1≥(r−1)L12.L2⋯Ln−1=0,2r\int_{X}c_{2}({\mathcal{E}})L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}\geq(r-1)L_{1}^{2}.L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0,

where r=rkℰr={\mathop{\rm rk\,}}{\mathcal{E}}. If A.L2⋯Ln−1A.L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1} is numerically trivial, then A2.L2⋯Ln−1=0A^{2}.L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0. Nefness implies that L2⋯Ln−1L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1} has zero intersection with every codimension-two cycle. Singular Riemann–Roch therefore gives

χ(X,c1(L2)⋯c1(Ln−1)⋅ℱ)=0\chi\left(X,c_{1}(L_{2})\cdots c_{1}(L_{n-1})\cdot{\mathcal{F}}\right)=0

for every coherent sheaf ℱ{\mathcal{F}}. The asymptotic description of the second Chern class, together with L12.L2⋯Ln−1=0L_{1}^{2}.L_{2}\cdots L_{n-1}=0, gives the asserted vanishing.

For the last assertion, first suppose that L2,…,Ln−1L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1} are ample. For any ample divisor AA, generic semipositivity with respect to (L1+ϵ​A,L2,…,Ln−1)(L_{1}+\epsilon A,L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1}) for all rational ϵ>0\epsilon>0 implies generic semipositivity with respect to (L1,…,Ln−1)(L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-1}), by taking limits of the degrees of torsion free quotients, also after every reflexive Frobenius pullback in positive characteristic. Thus either (1) or (2) applies. The assertion for nef L2,…,Ln−1L_{2},\ldots,L_{n-1} follows by continuity. ∎

Corollary 5.11.

Let XX be a normal projective variety of dimension n≥2n\geq 2 over an algebraically closed field kk. Assume that KXK_{X} is nef and ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-Cartier and that ΩX[1]\Omega_{X}^{[1]} is generically semipositive. Then for any nef line bundles L1,…,Ln−2L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-2} on XX we have

∫Xc2(ΩX[1])L1⋯Ln−2≥0.\int_{X}c_{2}(\Omega_{X}^{[1]})L_{1}\cdots L_{n-2}\geq 0.

In characteristic zero, the generic semipositivity assumption can be replaced by the assumption that XX is non-uniruled.

Proof.

The first assertion follows from Theorem 5.10. For the second assertion we can assume that k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}. Let ΩX[1]→𝒬\Omega_{X}^{[1]}\to{\mathcal{Q}} be a nonzero torsion free quotient and let f:Y→Xf:Y\to X be a projective resolution which is an isomorphism over XregX_{\mathrm{reg}}. Saturating the extension of the kernel gives a torsion free quotient 𝒬~\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}} of ΩY1\Omega_{Y}^{1} with f∗​c1​(𝒬~)=c1​(𝒬)f_{*}c_{1}(\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}})=c_{1}({\mathcal{Q}}). Since YY is non-uniruled, [CP11, Theorem 0.1] implies that det𝒬~\det\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}} is pseudoeffective. Consequently, for any ample line bundles L1,…,Ln−1L_{1},\ldots,L_{n-1} on XX,

c1(𝒬).L1⋯Ln−1=c1(𝒬~).f∗L1⋯f∗Ln−1≥0.c_{1}({\mathcal{Q}}).L_{1}\cdots L_{n-1}=c_{1}(\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}}).f^{*}L_{1}\cdots f^{*}L_{n-1}\geq 0.

This proves generic semipositivity of ΩX[1]\Omega_{X}^{[1]}. ∎

Remark 5.12.

If XX is a smooth complex projective variety with KXK_{X} nef (or just pseudo-effective) then it is non-uniruled by [BDPP13]. However, this fails for general normal complex projective varieties (e.g., for a cone over a smooth projective quintic curve in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}).

5.4 Big reflexive sheaves and hyperbolicity

Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a reflexive sheaf of rank rr on a normal proper surface XX. We say that ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is big if

lim supm⟶∞h0​(X,Sym[m]ℰ)mr+1>0.\limsup_{m\longrightarrow\infty}\frac{h^{0}(X,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})}{m^{r+1}}>0.

The following theorem generalizes [Bog79, Corollary 10.11].

Theorem 5.13.

Let XX be a normal projective surface over an algebraically closed field kk. Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} be a reflexive sheaf of rank r≥1r\geq 1 on XX. Assume that ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is generically HH-semipositive for some ample HH. Then for every line bundle AA on XX we have

h0​(X,Sym[m]ℰ⊗A−1)≥∫Xs2​(ℰ)(r+1)!​mr+1−O⁡(mr).h^{0}\bigl(X,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\otimes A^{-1}\bigr)\geq\frac{\int_{X}s_{2}({\mathcal{E}})}{(r+1)!}\,m^{r+1}-O(m^{r}).

In particular, if ∫Xs2​(ℰ)>0\int_{X}s_{2}({\mathcal{E}})>0 then ℰ{\mathcal{E}} is big.

Proof.

By Corollary 3.3 we have

χ⁡(X,Sym[m]ℰ⊗A−1)=χ⁡(X,Sym[m]ℰ)+O⁡(mr)=∫Xs2​(ℰ)(r+1)!​mr+1+O⁡(mr).\chi(X,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\otimes A^{-1})=\chi(X,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})+O(m^{r})=\frac{\int_{X}s_{2}({\mathcal{E}})}{(r+1)!}\,m^{r+1}+O(m^{r}).

So it is sufficient to prove that h2​(X,Sym[m]ℰ⊗A−1)=O⁡(mr)h^{2}(X,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\otimes A^{-1})=O(m^{r}). But by Serre’s duality we have h2​(X,Sym[m]ℰ⊗A−1)=h0​(X,(Sym[m]ℰ)∗​⊗^​A​(KX)).h^{2}(X,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}}\otimes A^{-1})=h^{0}(X,({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})^{*}\hat{\otimes}A(K_{X})). By the Ramanan–Ramanathan theorem (see [Lan04a, Appendix]) we have

μmax,H​((Sym[m]ℰ)∗​⊗^​A​(KX))≤\displaystyle\mu_{\max,H}(({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})^{*}\hat{\otimes}A(K_{X}))\leq Lmax,H​((Sym[m]ℰ)∗​⊗^​A​(KX))\displaystyle L_{\max,H}(({\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{[m]}{\mathcal{E}})^{*}\hat{\otimes}A(K_{X}))
=−m​Lmin,H​(ℰ)+(KX+A)​H≤(KX+A)​H.\displaystyle=-mL_{\min,H}({\mathcal{E}})+(K_{X}+A)H\leq(K_{X}+A)H.

So the required inequality follows from the Le Potier–Simpson theorem (see [HL10, Theorem 3.3.1]) and its positive characteristic version (see [Lan04a, Corollary 3.4]). ∎

As a corollary, we obtain the following result, which in the smooth case was proven by Bogomolov in [Bog77].

Corollary 5.14.

Let XX be a normal projective surface over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. If XX is non-uniruled and ∫Xs2​(ΩX[1])>0\int_{X}s_{2}(\Omega_{X}^{[1]})>0 then ΩX[1]\Omega_{X}^{[1]} is big and there are only finitely many complete integral curves C⊂Xreg,C\subset X_{\mathrm{reg}}, whose normalizations have genus at most one.

Proof.

Since XX is non-uniruled, ΩX[1]\Omega_{X}^{[1]} is generically semipositive (see the proof of Corollary 5.11). Hence it is big by Theorem 5.13. In particular, there exist an ample line bundle AA, an integer m>0m>0, and a nonzero section

s∈H0​(Xreg,Symm⁡ΩXreg1⊗A−1).s\in H^{0}\!\left(X_{\mathrm{reg}},\operatorname{Sym}^{m}\Omega_{X_{\mathrm{reg}}}^{1}\otimes A^{-1}\right).

Then finiteness can be proven using Bogomolov’s arguments as in [Bog77, §5 and Theorem 2] (see also [Des79, Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.5]). ∎

The following example shows that the assumptions of Corollary 5.14 do not imply that a smooth projective resolution of XX has a big cotangent bundle.

Example 5.15.

Let BB be a complex abelian surface and let HH be a very ample divisor on BB. Fix an integer k≥2k\geq 2 and choose smooth curves C∈|k​H|C\in|kH| and D∈|(k+1)​H|D\in|(k+1)H| meeting transversely. Let π:Y→B\pi:Y\to B be the blow up of BB at the points of C∩DC\cap D. Let EE be the exceptional divisor and let C′C^{\prime} be the strict transform of CC. Then L=π∗​((k+1)​H)−EL=\pi^{*}((k+1)H)-E is globally generated and Stein’s factorization of the morphism defined by the linear system |L||L| gives a projective birational morphism f:Y→Xf:Y\to X onto a normal projective surface, contracting exactly C′C^{\prime}. Let AA be an ample line bundle on XX such that L=f∗​AL=f^{*}A. Since KB=0K_{B}=0, we have KY=E=k​L−(k+1)​C′.K_{Y}=E=kL-(k+1)C^{\prime}. The contracted point is singular, since C′C^{\prime} has positive genus. Restricting to Y∖C′≃XregY\setminus C^{\prime}\simeq X_{\mathrm{reg}} and taking reflexive extensions shows that ωX≃A⊗k\omega_{X}\simeq A^{\otimes k}. In particular, KXK_{X} is Cartier and ample, and the discrepancy of C′C^{\prime} is −(k+1)-(k+1). So we have

On the other hand, the symmetric plurigenera of smooth projective varieties are birational invariants and ΩB1≃𝒪B⊕2\Omega_{B}^{1}\simeq{\mathcal{O}}_{B}^{\oplus 2}, so h0​(Y,SymmΩY1)=m+1h^{0}(Y,{\mathop{{\rm Sym\,}}}^{m}\Omega_{Y}^{1})=m+1 and the cotangent bundle of YY, or of any smooth projective resolution of XX, is not big.

The following example coming from [GP15, Theorem 5.1] shows that in general, the assumptions of Corollary 5.14 do not imply that there are only finitely many integral curves C⊂X,C\subset X, whose normalizations have genus at most one.

Example 5.16.

Consider the smooth complex projective genus-two curve CC with an affine part given by y2=x5+1y^{2}=x^{5}+1 and the automorphism γ⁡(x,y)=(ζ5​x,y)\gamma(x,y)=(\zeta_{5}x,y) of CC, where ζ5\zeta_{5} is a primitive fifth root of unity. Appendix A Non-existence of a good theory of higher Chern classes

The second Chern classes (or Chern characters) constructed in this paper are compatible with finite pullbacks and the asymptotic Riemann–Roch formula. In higher degrees, the expected leading term in asymptotic Riemann–Roch is already incompatible with the usual duality formula, even without imposing any functoriality under pullbacks. The obstruction occurs for rank-one reflexive sheaves on a projective threefold.

For a rank-one reflexive sheaf ℒ{\mathcal{L}} we write ℒ[m]=(ℒ⊗m)∗⁣∗{\mathcal{L}}^{[m]}=({\mathcal{L}}^{\otimes m})^{**}.

Proposition A.1.

Let kk be an algebraically closed field and let n≥3n\geq 3. There is no assignment of a real number γX​(ℒ)\gamma_{X}({\mathcal{L}}) to every normal projective nn-dimensional variety XX over kk and every isomorphism class of rank-one reflexive sheaves ℒ{\mathcal{L}} on XX satisfying the following properties:

  1. 1.

    For every rank-one reflexive sheaf ℒ{\mathcal{L}}, γX​(ℒ∗)=(−1)n​γX​(ℒ).\gamma_{X}({\mathcal{L}}^{*})=(-1)^{n}\gamma_{X}({\mathcal{L}}).

  2. 2.

    For every rank-one reflexive sheaf ℒ{\mathcal{L}}, χ⁡(X,ℒ[m])=γX​(ℒ[m])+O⁡(mn−1).\chi(X,{\mathcal{L}}^{[m]})=\gamma_{X}({\mathcal{L}}^{[m]})+O(m^{n-1}).

Proof.

Since (ℒ[m])∗≃(ℒ∗)[m]({\mathcal{L}}^{[m]})^{*}\simeq({\mathcal{L}}^{*})^{[m]}, the two properties imply

χ⁡(X,ℒ[m])−(−1)n​χ​(X,(ℒ∗)[m])=O⁡(mn−1).\chi(X,{\mathcal{L}}^{[m]})-(-1)^{n}\chi(X,({\mathcal{L}}^{*})^{[m]})=O(m^{n-1}).

Consider the projective quadric cone X={x0x3−x1x2=0}⊂ℙk4X=\{x_{0}x_{3}-x_{1}x_{2}=0\}\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{4}_{k} and set D={x0=x1=0}⊂XD=\{x_{0}=x_{1}=0\}\subset X. One can easily check that for every integer m≥0m\geq 0 we have

χ⁡(X,𝒪X​(m​D))=m+1,χ⁡(X,𝒪X​(−m​D))=(m+13)−m+1.\chi(X,{\mathcal{O}}_{X}(mD))=m+1,\qquad\chi(X,{\mathcal{O}}_{X}(-mD))=\binom{m+1}{3}-m+1.

So for n=3n=3 and ℒ=𝒪X​(D){\mathcal{L}}={\mathcal{O}}_{X}(D) we have

χ⁡(X,ℒ[m])+χ⁡(X,(ℒ∗)[m])=(m+13)+2,\chi(X,{\mathcal{L}}^{[m]})+\chi(X,({\mathcal{L}}^{*})^{[m]})=\binom{m+1}{3}+2,

contradicting the required O⁡(m2)O(m^{2}) estimate. For n>3n>3, one can obtain a similar contradiction considering X×ℙn−3X\times{\mathbb{P}}^{n-3} and ℒ⊠𝒪ℙn−3​(1).{\mathcal{L}}\boxtimes{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{n-3}}(1). ∎

The intended invariant would be γX​(ℒ)=∫Xchn(ℒ)\gamma_{X}({\mathcal{L}})=\int_{X}{\mathop{\rm ch\,}}_{n}({\mathcal{L}}). Thus, in every degree n≥3n\geq 3, the usual duality formula and the expected leading term in asymptotic Riemann–Roch cannot hold simultaneously for all rank-one reflexive sheaves. The proof also works with an error o⁡(mn)o(m^{n}) in property (2).

Remark A.2.

A related failure of duality for pullbacks of Weil divisors was observed by de Fernex and Hacon [dFH09, Remark 2.11 and Example 2.12]. For a birational morphism f:Y→Xf:Y\to X of normal varieties, their natural pullback is characterized by

𝒪Y​(−f♮​D)=(𝒪X​(−D)⋅𝒪Y)∗⁣∗.{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}(-f^{\natural}D)=\bigl({\mathcal{O}}_{X}(-D)\cdot{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}\bigr)^{**}.

They show that f♮​(−D)≥−f♮​Df^{\natural}(-D)\geq-f^{\natural}D and that their asymptotic pullback can satisfy f∗​(−D)≠−f∗​Df^{*}(-D)\neq-f^{*}D. Their example exhibits a failure of pullback constructions to respect duality. Proposition A.1 concerns the compatibility of duality with asymptotic Euler characteristics.
